deep.reconstruction:
The page is a set of terse notes, not a derivation. Read top to bottom:

(1) a_n/n → ∞. This is a gap (lacunarity) condition on an increasing sequence of positive integers a_1 < a_2 < ...

(2) Σ x^{a_n}. This is the gap power series f(x) = Σ_{n≥1} x^{a_n}, which has radius of convergence 1.

(3) a_1, a_2, ... introduces the exponent sequence.

(4) a_{n+1} − a_n → ∞. This is a second, weaker-looking gap condition. A crossed-out scribble sits to its left in the margin.

(5) a_n = n^2 together with φ(n) = √n is the test example. With exponents the squares, f is the theta-type series Σ x^{n^2}. The function φ(n) = √n seems to be the conjectured or known bound for the exponential (Weyl) sums attached to the exponents.

(6) cos 1^2 x + cos 2^2 x + ... + cos n^2 x = O(√n). This is the real part of the quadratic Weyl sum S_n(x) = Σ_{k≤n} e^{i k^2 x}, the partial sums of the series in (2) on the unit circle at e^{ix}.

My interpretation (not on the page): the notes record the question of how the partial sums Σ_{k≤n} e^{i a_k θ} of a gap series grow on the unit circle. The question may also concern the boundary behaviour of Σ x^{a_n} as |x| → 1. In the model case a_n = n^2 the answer would be 'O(φ(n)) with φ(n) = √n'.

This is exactly the topic of Hardy–Littlewood, 'Some problems of Diophantine approximation II' (Acta Math. 37, 1914). They showed via the theta transformation that Σ_{k≤n} e^{πi k^2 θ} = O(√n) when θ has bounded partial quotients, and O(n^{1/2+ε}) for almost all θ. By Abel summation, O(√n) for the partial sums gives Σ r^{k^2} e^{ik^2 x} = O((1−r)^{−1/4}).

The condition a_n/n → ∞ is Fabry's gap condition (unit circle is a natural boundary). The condition a_{n+1} − a_n → ∞ is the gap condition in results on lacunary series (e.g. Fejér/Pólya, and later Ingham 1936). The page is plausibly notes from a discussion with Hardy around 1914–1919. No derivation is carried out.
errors: The statement cos 1^2 x + ... + cos n^2 x = O(√n) is not true for all x and no condition on x is written. At x = 0 the sum equals n. At x = π/2, cos(k^2 π/2) = 1 for even k and 0 for odd k, so the sum is about n/2. In general it fails at every rational multiple of π for which the Gauss sum does not vanish.

As written, O(√n) holds only for x/π (or x/2π) of bounded type, i.e. with bounded partial quotients (Hardy–Littlewood 1914). For almost all x one only gets O(n^{1/2+ε}), or Hardy–Littlewood's sharper O(√n log n)-type bounds. Presumably the restriction was understood but left unwritten.
The relation between the two gap conditions and the series Σ x^{a_n} is not stated, so no claim on the page can be checked beyond the cosine-sum example.

results.what: Gap power series Σ x^{a_n} with a_n/n → ∞
results.modern_name: Fabry gap theorem (lacunary series; unit circle is a natural boundary)

results.what: Gap condition a_{n+1} − a_n → ∞ for exponent sequences
results.modern_name: Lacunary / nonharmonic Fourier series gap conditions

results.what: Σ_{k≤n} cos(k^2 x) = O(√n) (for suitable x)
results.modern_name: Quadratic Weyl sum / theta-sum bound via approximate functional equation
results.usually_credited_to: Hardy & Littlewood 1914 (Acta Math. 37); also Weyl 1916 for equidistribution

deep.surprise_reason: These are fragmentary notes on well-known Hardy–Littlewood material (theta-type Weyl sums, gap series) contemporary with Ramanujan's stay in Cambridge. They carry no proof and no new claim, and the stated bound needs an unstated hypothesis on x.

checkable.asserts: At x = 0 the sum equals n, so O(sqrt(n)) cannot hold for all x (result 0).

checkable.sympy: [sum(cos(k**2*pi/2) for k in range(1, N+1)) for N in (10, 100)]
checkable.asserts: At x = pi/2 the sum is about N/2 (5 and 50), a counterexample to an unrestricted O(sqrt(n)).

checkable.sympy: max(abs(sum(cos(k**2*pi*(sqrt(5)-1)).evalf() for k in range(1, N+1)))/sqrt(N) for N in range(1, 2001, 100))
checkable.asserts: For x = π·(√5−1) (so x/π has bounded partial quotients), the ratio |S_N|/√N stays bounded, consistent with Hardy–Littlewood.
At x = π, cos(k^2 π) = (−1)^k, so the partial sums are bounded (0 at even N).

transcription_corrections: There is a crossed-out scribble in the left margin beside 'a_{n+1} − a_n → ∞'; the transcription omits it.
The last line reads 'cos 1^2 x + ... + cos n^2 x = O√n'; it should be rendered as O(√n), with x the variable rather than 't'.
There is a trailing period after Σ x^{a_n} and a semicolon after ∞ in the first line; these are punctuation only.
